levels.title: Start from zero
levels.description: Your first words, greetings, and simple sentences.

levels.name: A1
levels.title: Everyday foundations
levels.description: Handle familiar routines, messages, and conversations.

levels.name: A2
levels.title: Find your confidence
levels.description: Talk about experiences, travel, and what comes next.

levels.name: B1
levels.title: Independent English
levels.description: Explain your views and connect ideas with confidence.

levels.name: B2
levels.title: Express yourself clearly
levels.description: Build persuasive arguments and begin IELTS-style work.

levels.name: C1
levels.title: Advanced expression
levels.description: Understand nuance and develop academic communication.

levels.name: C2
levels.title: Precision & mastery

levels.name: Biz
levels.title: Business English
levels.description: Professional communication for the modern workplace.

lessons.title: Hello, I am…
lessons.description: Build your first English sentences with the verb be.

content.heading: Meet the verb be
content.text: Use be to give a name, describe a person, or say where someone is. The form changes with the subject: I am, you are, he is, she is, it is, we are, they are. A simple statement normally has a subject and a verb.
examples: I am Maya.
You are a student.
She is at home.

content.heading: Short forms and negatives
content.text: In conversation, I am becomes I’m, you are becomes you’re, and she is becomes she’s. To make a negative statement, put not after be. Start a yes-or-no question with be, then the subject. Read each pair aloud to hear the change.
examples: I’m happy. / I’m not tired.
You are ready. → Are you ready?
Is he a teacher? Yes, he is.

questions.prompt: Choose the complete sentence.
questions.explanation: I takes am. A complete sentence includes the subject I and the verb am.

questions.prompt: Maya and Ben ___ at home.
questions.explanation: Maya and Ben means they, so use are.

questions.prompt: Which question is correct?
questions.explanation: For a standard question with be, put the verb before the subject: Are you ready?

lessons.title: Words around you
lessons.description: Name everyday things, people, and numbers.

content.heading: People and things
content.text: A noun names a person, place, or thing. Begin with words you can see around you: teacher, student, book, pen, door, and chair. Say the word, point to the thing, then use it in a short sentence. Use a before a consonant sound and an before a vowel sound.
examples: a book / a teacher
an apple / an egg
This is a chair.

content.heading: One or more than one
content.text: One book is singular. Two books is plural. Most everyday nouns add s in the plural. Learn numbers from one to ten, then use them to count real objects. Some common nouns change differently: one person becomes two people.
examples: one pen → three pens
one apple → five apples
one person → two people

questions.prompt: Which word names something you can write with?
questions.explanation: A pen is a tool for writing.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct phrase.
questions.explanation: Apple begins with a vowel sound, so use an.

questions.prompt: What is the plural of person?
questions.explanation: The usual plural for individual human beings is people: two people.

lessons.title: Read your first story
lessons.description: Find names, places, and simple facts in a short text.

content.heading: Read for the main idea
content.text: Read this short introduction twice: “My name is Ali. I am a student. I live in Kandy. My friend is Sara. She is a teacher.” On your first reading, ask who the text is about. You do not need to translate every word to understand the main idea.
examples: The text introduces Ali.
Ali is a student.
Sara is Ali’s friend.

content.heading: Look for a specific fact
content.text: On your second reading, look for one piece of information at a time. Who asks about a person; where asks about a place; what often asks about a thing or job. Go back to the text to check your answer instead of guessing from memory.
examples: Who is a teacher? Sara.
Where does Ali live? In Kandy.
What is Ali? A student.

questions.prompt: According to the text, who is a student?
questions.explanation: The text says, “My name is Ali. I am a student.”

questions.prompt: Where does Ali live?
questions.explanation: Ali says, “I live in Kandy.”

questions.prompt: Which sentence matches the text?
questions.explanation: The final sentence describes Sara: “She is a teacher.”

lessons.title: Listen: meet a new friend
lessons.description: Hear a greeting and pick out a name and number.
lessons.listeningText: Hello! My name is Nina. I am a student. I am twenty years old. My class is in room four. Nice to meet you!

content.heading: Listen once for the situation
content.text: Use the play button to hear Nina’s introduction. First listen without pausing. Is the speaker introducing herself, buying food, or asking for directions? Your first goal is to understand the situation. A greeting such as hello often tells you a conversation is beginning.
examples: Hello! My name is Nina.
Nice to meet you.
Hi! I’m Ben.

content.heading: Listen again for details
content.text: On your second listen, focus on a name, age, or room number. Say the numbers four, fourteen, and forty slowly; they are different words. If you miss something in real life, ask the speaker to repeat it. Listening improves through repeated, focused practice.
examples: My class is in room four.
Could you say that again, please?
How do you spell your name?

questions.prompt: What is the speaker’s name?
questions.explanation: The introduction begins, “My name is Nina.”

questions.prompt: How old is Nina?
questions.explanation: She says, “I am twenty years old.”

questions.prompt: Which room is her class in?
questions.explanation: The class is in room four. Listen for the whole number.

lessons.title: Your first three sentences
lessons.description: Use capitals, spaces, and full stops to introduce yourself.

content.heading: Give every sentence a clear shape
content.text: Start a sentence with a capital letter and end a statement with a full stop. Leave a space between words. The word I is always capitalized, even in the middle of a sentence. Names and places also begin with capitals. These small habits make your message easy to read.
examples: My name is Ravi.
I am a student.
I live in Galle.

content.heading: Write, read, and check
content.text: Write three true sentences: your name, where you live, and one thing about yourself. Read each one aloud. Check that it has a subject and a verb, begins with a capital, and ends with punctuation. You can replace the examples with your own details.
examples: My name is ___.
I live in ___.
I am happy to learn English.

questions.prompt: Which sentence uses capitals correctly?
questions.explanation: Capitalize the first word and the person’s name: My name is Maya.

questions.prompt: Choose the best way to finish this statement: “I live in Galle”
questions.explanation: A statement ends with a full stop, and the words need spaces.

questions.prompt: Which is a complete sentence?
questions.explanation: I am a new student has a subject, I, and a verb, am.

lessons.title: Say hello with confidence
lessons.description: Practice a short, friendly introduction and take turns.

content.heading: Learn a small conversation
content.text: You can start speaking with a few useful chunks. A chunk is a group of words you remember together. Say hello, give your name, and ask the other person’s name. Practice slowly first, then say the conversation again with a natural pause after each sentence.
examples: Hello, I’m Maya. What’s your name?
I’m Sam. Nice to meet you.
Nice to meet you, too.

content.heading: Be clear and keep going
content.text: You do not need a perfect accent to communicate. Speak at a comfortable speed and make your key words clear. If you do not understand, ask for repetition. Practice your introduction out loud three times, changing one detail each time. If recording is available, listen and notice one thing to improve.
examples: Sorry, could you repeat that?
I’m from Sri Lanka.
And you?

questions.prompt: Someone says, “Nice to meet you.” What is a natural reply?
questions.explanation: Nice to meet you, too is a friendly response when meeting someone.

questions.prompt: You did not understand a name. What can you say?
questions.explanation: Politely ask the person to repeat the information.

questions.prompt: Which question invites the other person to introduce themselves?
questions.explanation: What’s your name? asks the other person for their name.

lessons.title: Talk about your routine
lessons.description: Use the present simple for habits, facts, and questions.

content.heading: Habits and everyday facts
content.text: Use the present simple for regular activities and facts. Use the base verb with I, you, we, and they. Add s or es with he, she, and it. Frequency words such as usually and often normally go before the main verb, but after be.
examples: I study every evening.
She studies every evening.
He is usually early.

content.heading: Questions and negatives with do
content.text: Use do or does to ask present simple questions. Use don’t or doesn’t for negatives. After does or doesn’t, the main verb returns to its base form. Ask about a partner’s routine and answer with a time or frequency to make your meaning more useful.
examples: Do you work on Saturdays?
Does she live near here?
He doesn’t drink coffee.

questions.prompt: My sister ___ English every day.
questions.explanation: My sister is she, so use studies in the present simple.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct question.
questions.explanation: Use does with he and the base verb work.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is correct?
questions.explanation: Doesn’t already marks the third person, so the main verb stays like.

lessons.title: Food, home & your neighbourhood
lessons.description: Use practical words and natural combinations every day.

content.heading: Learn words in useful pairs
content.text: Learn a word together with words that often go with it. We make breakfast, take a bus, and buy groceries. A supermarket sells food and household items; a pharmacy sells medicines; a library lends books. Imagine your own neighbourhood as you use each word.
examples: I buy groceries at the supermarket.
The pharmacy is next to the bank.
I take a bus to work.

content.heading: Countable and uncountable nouns
content.text: You can count apples and eggs: one apple, two eggs. Words such as rice, water, and bread are usually uncountable when we describe food in general. Use some or a quantity phrase such as a bottle of water. In negative sentences and questions, any is often useful.
examples: We have some rice.
Do you have any eggs?
I’d like a bottle of water.

questions.prompt: Where would you normally borrow a book?
questions.explanation: A library lets people borrow books.

questions.prompt: Choose the natural phrase.
questions.explanation: Take a bus is a common combination for travelling by bus.

questions.prompt: Which request is correct?
questions.explanation: A bottle of water uses a countable container to measure water.

lessons.title: Read the message, find the plan
lessons.description: Understand practical texts, opening times, and invitations.

content.heading: Read a useful everyday message
content.text: Read this message: “Hi Ana! Let’s meet at the library on Saturday at 10 a.m. Bring your English notebook. The café next door is closed, so we can have lunch at my house afterward. —Leo.” Look for the people, place, day, and time before you focus on smaller details.
examples: Who is writing? Leo.
Where will they meet? At the library.
When? Saturday at 10 a.m.

content.heading: Notice a change or a reason
content.text: Small words connect important details. So often introduces a result; because gives a reason; but shows a contrast. In Leo’s message, the closed café explains why lunch is at home. Do not assume that a familiar place is the final meeting place: check the actual words.
examples: The café is closed, so lunch is at Leo’s house.
Bring your English notebook.
Afterward means after the library visit.

questions.prompt: Where will Ana and Leo first meet?
questions.explanation: Leo says, “Let’s meet at the library.”

questions.prompt: What should Ana bring?
questions.explanation: The message directly asks Ana to bring her English notebook.

questions.prompt: Why will they have lunch at Leo’s house?
options: The café next door is closed.
questions.explanation: The word so links the closed café to their plan to eat at Leo’s house.

lessons.title: Listen: a change of plan
lessons.description: Understand times, days, and a simple corrected arrangement.
lessons.listeningText: Hi Eva, it is Tom. Our English class is usually on Tuesday, but this week it is on Thursday. It starts at half past five, not five o’clock. Please meet me outside the library at five fifteen. Bring your notebook. See you there!

content.heading: Listen for the final information
content.text: Speakers sometimes mention an old plan before giving the new one. Listen for but, actually, or not: they can signal a correction. In this message, first identify what Tom is talking about. Then replay it and write the final day, class time, and meeting time.
examples: usually on Tuesday, but this week on Thursday
half past five = 5:30
five fifteen = 5:15

content.heading: Separate meeting time and start time
content.text: A message can contain more than one useful time. Label your notes: meet, start, and finish. This prevents you from choosing a correct number for the wrong event. After listening, repeat the plan in one sentence using your own words.
examples: Meet: outside the library, 5:15.
Class starts: 5:30 on Thursday.
Tom asks Eva to bring a notebook.

questions.prompt: Which day is the class this week?
questions.explanation: Tuesday is the usual day, but this week the class is on Thursday.

questions.prompt: What time does the class start?
questions.explanation: Half past five means 5:30.

questions.prompt: Where should Eva meet Tom?
questions.explanation: Tom says, “Please meet me outside the library.”

lessons.title: Write a friendly message
lessons.description: Make an invitation with a clear place, time, and question.

content.heading: Give your reader the essentials
content.text: A helpful invitation says what you want to do, where, and when. Begin with a greeting and use short sentences. Finish with a question so the reader knows how to reply. Your message can sound friendly without using complicated words.
examples: Hi Amira! Would you like to study together?
Let’s meet at the library on Friday at 4 p.m.
Are you free then?

content.heading: Link ideas and check the details
content.text: Use and to add information, but for a contrast, and because for a reason. Before sending your message, check the person’s name, day, time, and place. Write a 40–60 word invitation to a friend, including what they should bring and how they can reply.
examples: Bring your notebook and a pen.
I can come on Friday, but I can’t come on Saturday.
Let’s go early because the library closes at six.

questions.prompt: Which invitation gives the clearest plan?
options: Let’s meet at the library on Friday at 4 p.m.
questions.explanation: The sentence gives an activity, a place, a day, and a time.

questions.prompt: Choose the best connector: “I can come on Friday, ___ I can’t come on Saturday.”
questions.explanation: But joins two contrasting ideas.

questions.prompt: Which ending invites a useful reply?
options: Are you free at that time?
questions.explanation: The question lets your friend confirm whether the plan works.

lessons.title: Order, ask & say thank you
lessons.description: Practice polite requests in cafés and everyday places.

content.heading: Ask politely and specifically
content.text: Use I’d like to request something and could I to ask politely. Add please naturally. A short, clear request is enough. In a café, say the item and quantity; in a shop, name the item or ask where it is. Practice both the customer and assistant roles.
examples: I’d like a tea, please.
Could I have two sandwiches?
Excuse me, where is the bus stop?

content.heading: Check that you understood
content.text: Repeat important information to confirm it. If a price, size, or direction is unclear, ask a short follow-up question. Say thank you when the other person helps. Focus on communicating the request clearly; you can improve pronunciation by repeating the same conversation with different items.
examples: Is that five pounds?
A small coffee, please.
Thank you for your help.

questions.prompt: Which is a polite café order?
questions.explanation: I’d like… please is a standard polite request.

questions.prompt: You did not hear the price. What is the best response?
options: Could you say the price again, please?
questions.explanation: Ask directly and politely for the missing information.

questions.prompt: Which phrase politely gets a stranger’s attention?
questions.explanation: Excuse me is a useful way to begin a polite request for help.

lessons.title: Yesterday, today, tomorrow
lessons.description: Describe past events and future intentions clearly.

content.heading: Finished actions in the past
content.text: Use the past simple for a finished action at a finished time. Regular verbs often add ed; common irregular forms include went, saw, and bought. Use did for questions and didn’t for negatives, followed by the base verb. A time phrase helps your listener place the event.
examples: We visited Galle last weekend.
She went by train.
Did you enjoy the journey?

content.heading: Plans and intentions
content.text: Use be going to plus a base verb for an intention or a plan already made. Keep the form of be matched to the subject. Compare your last weekend with your next one. Time expressions such as yesterday and next Saturday make the change of tense easier to follow.
examples: I’m going to study tonight.
They aren’t going to travel tomorrow.
Are you going to call her?

questions.prompt: We ___ to the beach last Sunday.
questions.explanation: Last Sunday is a finished past time; the past of go is went.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct past question.
questions.explanation: After did, use the base form buy.

questions.prompt: Which sentence describes a future intention?
options: I’m going to visit her tomorrow.
questions.explanation: Be going to plus visit describes a planned future action.

lessons.title: Travel without getting lost
lessons.description: Learn transport, accommodation, and travel problem vocabulary.

content.heading: From booking to arrival
content.text: Travel words become easier when you learn them in order: book a ticket, pack a suitcase, check in, board the train, and arrive at your destination. A departure is when a service leaves; an arrival is when it reaches a place. Use the correct preposition with common destinations.
examples: The train departs at nine.
We arrived at the station early.
They arrived in Paris yesterday.

content.heading: Explain a small problem
content.text: A delay means something happens later than planned; a cancellation means it will not happen. A reservation is an arrangement to keep a room or seat for you. State the problem, give an identifying detail, then ask for help. Learn complete phrases so you can use them quickly.
examples: My train is delayed.
I have a reservation under the name Perera.
Could you help me find platform three?

questions.prompt: A train is delayed. What does that mean?
options: It will leave or arrive later than planned.
questions.explanation: A delay changes the timing; it does not necessarily mean a cancellation.

questions.prompt: Choose the natural phrase.
questions.explanation: Book a ticket means reserve or buy a place for a journey.

questions.prompt: Which sentence uses arrive correctly?
questions.explanation: Use arrive at for a specific place such as a station; use arrive in for a city or country.

lessons.title: Compare two useful options
lessons.description: Read for conditions, prices, and the best fit.

content.heading: Read the details that matter
content.text: Compare these classes. “Morning English: Monday and Wednesday, 9–10 a.m., £40 per month. Beginners welcome. Online only. Evening English: Tuesday and Thursday, 6–7:30 p.m., £55 per month. Some English needed. Classroom lessons; materials included.” First decide what you need, then locate details that match.
examples: Morning English is cheaper.
Evening English meets in a classroom.
Both classes meet twice a week.

content.heading: Do not add information
content.text: A text may not answer every question. Materials are explicitly included in the evening class, but the text does not say whether they are included in the morning class. Separate a stated fact from an assumption. When comparing choices, mention both your requirement and the supporting detail.
examples: A complete beginner can choose Morning English.
The text does not name either teacher.
Someone working mornings may prefer the evening option.

questions.prompt: Which class explicitly welcomes complete beginners?
questions.explanation: Morning English says “Beginners welcome”; evening students need some English.

questions.prompt: How much more does Evening English cost each month?
questions.explanation: £55 minus £40 is £15.

questions.prompt: What can we say about materials for Morning English?
questions.explanation: Only the evening description mentions materials. Missing information is not the same as a negative fact.

lessons.title: Listen: find your way
lessons.description: Follow directions and notice a temporary change.
lessons.listeningText: To get to the museum, walk straight along King Street. Turn left at the bank, then take the second right. The museum is opposite the park. The main entrance is closed today, so use the side entrance beside the café. The museum closes at four thirty this afternoon, an hour earlier than usual.

content.heading: Turn words into a route
content.text: For directions, listen for action words and landmarks. Straight, left, right, opposite, and beside tell you how places relate to each other. Sketch a simple route while listening. A landmark such as a bank is often easier to remember than a street number.
examples: Go straight along King Street.
Turn left at the bank.
Opposite means on the other side, facing it.

content.heading: Catch the practical change
content.text: Announcements often add an exception after the main information. Listen for today, closed, instead, and earlier. These details can change what you need to do. Replay the final sentences and check the entrance and closing time separately.
examples: Use the side entrance beside the café.
Today’s closing time: 4:30 p.m.
An hour earlier means one hour before the usual time.

questions.prompt: Where should you turn left?
questions.explanation: The direction is “Turn left at the bank.”

questions.prompt: Which entrance should visitors use today?
options: The side entrance beside the café
questions.explanation: The main entrance is closed, so visitors should use the side entrance.

questions.prompt: What time does the museum close today?
questions.explanation: The speaker says four thirty. The usual closing time is one hour later.

lessons.title: Tell a short story
lessons.description: Organize a real experience with a beginning, middle, and end.

content.heading: Put events in a clear order
content.text: A short personal story needs a setting, events, and a result. Begin with when and where. Use the past simple for the main finished events. Link them with first, then, after that, and finally. Choose only the details your reader needs to follow what happened.
examples: Last Saturday, I visited a friend in Galle.
First, we explored the old town.
After that, we had lunch near the sea.

content.heading: Add a feeling and revise
content.text: A final sentence about your feelings gives the story a natural ending. Write 80–100 words about a journey, celebration, or surprising day. Then check the order of events, past verb forms, spelling, and punctuation. Replace repeated words only when another word keeps the same meaning.
examples: We missed the bus, so we walked home.
I felt tired, but I was happy.
It was a day I will remember.

questions.prompt: Which is the strongest opening for a short past story?
options: Last Sunday, my family visited the beach.
questions.explanation: The opening establishes when, who, and where.

questions.prompt: Choose the logical order.
questions.explanation: First begins the sequence, then adds the next event, and finally introduces the last event.

questions.prompt: Which ending adds a feeling about the experience?
options: I felt proud because I tried something new.
questions.explanation: The sentence reflects on how the experience affected the writer.

lessons.title: Describe it, compare it
lessons.description: Talk about places and experiences with useful supporting details.

content.heading: Give more than a one-word answer
content.text: Answer the question directly, add a reason, and give a small example. This simple pattern helps a listener follow you. Practice describing your town, a favourite meal, or a recent trip for 30–45 seconds. Pause between ideas instead of rushing through one long sentence.
examples: I like my town because it is peaceful.
For example, there is a quiet park near my house.
Last week, I went there with my sister.

content.heading: Compare with a clear basis
content.text: Use adjective plus er for many short adjectives and more plus adjective for many longer ones. Use than to introduce the second thing. Name the feature you are comparing: price, size, comfort, or speed. Remember common irregular forms: good becomes better and bad becomes worse.
examples: The train is cheaper than a taxi.
This hotel is more comfortable.
The new route is better for me.

questions.prompt: Which answer develops “Do you like your town?” best?
options: Yes, because it is peaceful and I can walk to a lovely park.
questions.explanation: It answers directly and supports the answer with a reason and detail.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct comparison.
options: A train is cheapest than a taxi.
A train is cheaper than a taxi.
A train is cheap that a taxi.
A train is more cheap a taxi.
questions.explanation: Use the comparative cheaper followed by than.

questions.prompt: What is the comparative form of good?
questions.explanation: Better is the irregular comparative of good.

lessons.title: Connect experience & possibility
lessons.description: Distinguish the present perfect, past simple, and first conditional.

content.heading: Experience and a finished past time
content.text: Use the present perfect, have or has plus a past participle, for experience up to now or a past event connected to the present. Use the past simple with a finished past time such as yesterday or in 2022. Ever and never often ask about or describe life experience.
examples: I have visited India twice.
I visited Delhi in 2022.
Have you ever spoken to a large audience?

content.heading: A real future possibility
content.text: Use the first conditional for a possible future situation and its likely result: if plus present simple, then will plus base verb. The if-clause can come first or second. When it comes first, a comma normally separates the clauses. The present form after if can refer to the future.
examples: If I finish early, I will call you.
We will walk if it doesn’t rain.
If you practise regularly, you will feel more confident.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct sentence about a finished time.
questions.explanation: Yesterday is a finished past time, so use the past simple met.

questions.prompt: Which question asks about life experience up to now?
options: Did you surf at nine yesterday?
questions.explanation: Have you ever… asks whether the experience has happened at any time before now.

questions.prompt: If it rains tomorrow, we ___ at home.
questions.explanation: A real future possibility normally uses if plus present simple and will plus base verb.

lessons.title: Work smarter with words
lessons.description: Use workplace collocations, word families, and phrasal verbs.

content.heading: Remember the company a word keeps
content.text: A collocation is a common word combination. At work or school, we meet a deadline, gain experience, make progress, and take responsibility. Learning whole combinations makes your English more natural and reduces the number of decisions you need to make while speaking.
examples: We need to meet the deadline on Friday.
She gained experience as a volunteer.
You are making steady progress.

content.heading: Build families and notice meaning
content.text: Words in a family have different grammatical jobs: decide is a verb, decision is a noun, and decisive is an adjective. Phrasal verbs combine a verb with another word and can have a new meaning. Learn them in a sentence and check whether the situation is formal or informal.
examples: We need to make a decision.
Please fill in this form.
Let’s find out why the website stopped working.

questions.prompt: Which phrase means finish work by the required date?
questions.explanation: Meet a deadline means complete the work on time.

questions.prompt: Choose the noun: “We need to make a ___ today.”
questions.explanation: After make a, the noun decision is needed.

questions.prompt: “Please fill in this form” means…
options: write the requested information in it.
questions.explanation: Fill in a form means complete its empty spaces with information.

lessons.title: Find the claim & the evidence
lessons.description: Separate a writer’s opinion from the support offered for it.

content.heading: Read a short argument
content.text: Read this paragraph: “Our town should improve its bus service. In a recent survey of 200 residents, 120 said they would use buses more often if services ran after 8 p.m. A later service could help workers travel home without a car. However, the council must estimate the running costs before making a decision.” Identify the recommendation before examining its support.
examples: Claim: improve the town’s bus service.
Evidence: 120 of 200 respondents said they would use later buses more often.
Limitation: running costs still need examination.

content.heading: Keep the strength of the evidence in view
content.text: A survey can tell us what respondents said; it does not prove what every resident will do. Could expresses a possibility, while will is stronger. However introduces a qualification. Good readers notice both the writer’s position and the limits acknowledged in the argument.
examples: 120 out of 200 is 60% of the respondents.
Could help does not mean will definitely help.
The writer supports improvement while recognizing a cost question.

questions.prompt: What is the writer’s main recommendation?
questions.explanation: The first sentence states that the town should improve its bus service.

questions.prompt: What does the survey directly show?
options: 120 respondents said they would use later buses more often.
Later buses will make a profit.
questions.explanation: The survey reports the intentions of its respondents; the other claims go beyond the text.

questions.prompt: Why does the writer use however?
options: To add a concern about the costs.
questions.explanation: However marks a qualification: the cost needs to be assessed before a decision.

lessons.title: Listen: what do they really prefer?
lessons.description: Follow reasons, contrasts, and a final decision.
lessons.listeningText: I thought the online course would be easier because I would not have to travel. The recorded lessons were useful, especially when I wanted to review a difficult topic. Still, I missed being able to ask questions immediately. Next term, I am choosing a course that combines online materials with a weekly classroom session. It costs a little more, but the chance to discuss things with a teacher makes it worth it for me.

content.heading: Track a changing view
content.text: A speaker’s first opinion may not be their final one. Listen to the full explanation before choosing an answer. In this account, the speaker begins with an expectation, describes an advantage and a problem, then explains a decision. Words such as still and but reveal contrasts.
examples: Expectation: online study would be easier.
Benefit: recordings could be reviewed.
Problem: questions could not be asked immediately.

content.heading: Connect preferences to reasons
content.text: When taking notes, put a reason next to each opinion. This helps you distinguish the speaker’s actual preference from a detail mentioned in passing. Finally, summarize the decision in one sentence without repeating every example.
examples: Choice: a course with online and classroom learning.
Reason: access to discussion with a teacher.
The higher price is acceptable to this speaker.

questions.prompt: What did the speaker find useful about recorded lessons?
options: They were shorter than every class.
questions.explanation: The speaker says recordings were useful for reviewing a difficult topic.

questions.prompt: What was the main disadvantage mentioned?
options: The speaker could not ask questions immediately.
The course required too much travel.
questions.explanation: The speaker missed being able to ask questions immediately.

questions.prompt: What will the speaker choose next term?
options: A course combining online materials and classroom sessions
questions.explanation: The final decision is a combined format with a weekly classroom session.

lessons.title: Build a convincing paragraph
lessons.description: Connect a point, explanation, example, and final thought.

content.heading: One paragraph, one main idea
content.text: Start with a topic sentence that states your point. Explain why it matters, then add a specific example. Finish by linking the example to your point. The example may be a realistic illustration; do not present invented research or statistics as evidence. Clear development matters more than impressive words.
examples: Point: Libraries provide important study spaces.
Explanation: Some students cannot find quiet space at home.
Example: A student sharing a small room can work at a library desk.

content.heading: Make the connections visible
content.text: Use because for reasons, for example for illustrations, and therefore for results. Avoid adding a connector to every sentence. Write 100–130 words about whether schools should offer more practical subjects. Then underline your topic sentence and check that every remaining sentence develops the same point.
examples: Libraries are useful because they provide quiet work areas.
For example, students can prepare for exams there.
Therefore, extending opening hours could support local learners.

questions.prompt: What is the main job of a topic sentence?
options: To state the paragraph’s central point
questions.explanation: A topic sentence gives the reader the main idea the paragraph will develop.

questions.prompt: Which detail best supports “Libraries help students study”?
options: A bus passes a different building.
They provide quiet desks for students with limited space at home.
questions.explanation: Quiet study space directly explains how a library helps students.

questions.prompt: You have no source for a statistic. What should you do?
options: Use a clearly framed example or find a reliable source.
questions.explanation: An illustrative example can support an explanation without falsely claiming research evidence.

lessons.title: Keep the conversation flowing
lessons.description: Extend answers, repair mistakes, and ask useful follow-up questions.

content.heading: Answer, explain, illustrate
content.text: To develop an answer, make your point, explain it, and add an example. You can also compare past and present or describe a possible future. A brief pause is natural. Aim for understandable ideas at a steady pace rather than filling every second with words.
examples: I prefer studying in the morning because I concentrate better.
For instance, I usually finish difficult reading before lunch.
When I was younger, I tended to study late at night.

content.heading: Repair without restarting
content.text: If you use the wrong word or lose your place, correct the important part and continue. If you do not know a word, describe its function or appearance. Ask a follow-up question to show interest in the other person. These strategies keep communication moving while you build vocabulary.
examples: What I mean is…
It’s a device you use to measure temperature.
That sounds interesting. How did you get started?

questions.prompt: Which response develops an opinion most clearly?
options: It is difficult to say anything.
I prefer mornings because I concentrate better; for example, I do my reading before lunch.
questions.explanation: The answer includes a preference, a reason, and an example.

questions.prompt: You forget the word thermometer. What is a useful strategy?
options: Describe it as a device for measuring temperature.
questions.explanation: Describing a word’s function is a useful paraphrasing strategy.

questions.prompt: Which phrase helps you clarify your own meaning?
questions.explanation: What I mean is… signals a clarification or repair.

lessons.title: Change the focus of a sentence
lessons.description: Use the passive and reported speech with control.

content.heading: Focus on the action or result
content.text: The passive uses a form of be plus the past participle. Use it when the action or result matters more than the person doing it, or when that person is unknown. Keep the tense in the form of be. Include a by-phrase only when the agent is useful information.
examples: Someone repaired the bridge. → The bridge was repaired.
The results will be published tomorrow.
The report has been reviewed by two specialists.

content.heading: Report what someone said
content.text: Reported speech gives someone’s message without reproducing the exact words. After a past reporting verb, a tense often moves back and pronouns or time expressions may change. Backshift depends on context: a fact still true can remain in the present. Tell normally needs a person; say does not.
examples: “I am tired,” she said. → She said she was tired.
He told me the meeting had ended.
She said the office opens at nine.

questions.prompt: Choose the passive of “They will publish the results tomorrow.”
options: The results will be published tomorrow.
questions.explanation: Future passive uses will be plus the past participle published.

questions.prompt: Which report is grammatically correct?
options: He said me the meeting had ended.
He tell me the meeting had ended.
He told me that the meeting had ended.
He told that the meeting had ended.
questions.explanation: Tell takes a person, such as me; the past form is told.

questions.prompt: Why might a writer choose “The window was broken”?
options: To avoid using any verb tense.
To focus on the event when the person responsible is unknown or unimportant.
To describe an action that must happen tomorrow.
questions.explanation: The passive changes the focus; it does not prove the action had no agent.

lessons.title: Choose the word that fits
lessons.description: Use precise collocations and match the level of formality.

content.heading: Precision beats unnecessary complexity
content.text: Near-synonyms are not always interchangeable. Raise awareness is natural, while lift awareness is not a usual combination. A significant change is important or large in context; it does not always mean statistically significant. Check meaning, grammar, and collocation before replacing a familiar word with a sophisticated one.
examples: raise awareness of road safety
conduct research into language learning
a significant improvement in clarity

content.heading: Match your reader and purpose
content.text: Register is the level and style of language appropriate to a situation. A friendly message can use find out; a formal report may use investigate. Neither is automatically better. Avoid mixing very casual expressions into a formal request unless you have a clear reason.
examples: Informal: Can you look into this?
Formal: Could you investigate this issue?
Neutral: Please let me know the result.

questions.prompt: Which is the natural collocation?
questions.explanation: Raise awareness is the conventional combination for increasing public understanding.

questions.prompt: Which sentence best suits a formal report?
options: Hey, the numbers are kind of wild.
The team investigated the cause of the decline.
The team did stuff to the numbers.
We checked the thing out and it was super weird.
questions.explanation: Investigated and cause of the decline are precise and appropriate for a formal report.

questions.prompt: When is a less familiar synonym a good replacement?
options: When its meaning, grammar, and usual combinations fit the context.
questions.explanation: Vocabulary control depends on accurate use in context, not word length.

lessons.title: IELTS-style reading: evidence first
lessons.description: Practice skimming, scanning, and True/False/Not Given reasoning.

content.heading: Skim, then locate the evidence
content.text: Read this original practice passage: “A city pilot introduced rooftop gardens on five public buildings. Staff reported that the gardens made the buildings more pleasant. Sensors recorded lower roof-surface temperatures on hot afternoons. The pilot did not measure electricity use, and the council has not yet decided whether to extend the project.” Skim for the overall topic, then scan for the detail each question needs.
examples: Main topic: a rooftop garden pilot.
Measured: roof-surface temperatures.
Not measured: electricity use.

content.heading: False is different from missing
content.text: In True/False/Not Given tasks, True agrees with the passage, False contradicts it, and Not Given means the passage does not provide enough information. Do not use your outside knowledge to fill gaps. A benefit that sounds plausible is still unconfirmed if the passage does not establish it.
examples: “The pilot involved five buildings” agrees with the passage.
“Electricity use was measured” contradicts the passage.
“The gardens cost £50,000” is not established.

questions.prompt: “The pilot measured electricity use.” Which judgement is supported?
questions.explanation: The passage explicitly says the pilot did not measure electricity use, so the statement is false.

questions.prompt: “The gardens cost £50,000.” Which judgement is supported?
questions.explanation: The passage provides no cost figure, so the statement is not given.

questions.prompt: Which conclusion stays within the evidence?
options: All city buildings now have gardens.
Roof-surface temperatures were lower on hot afternoons.
The project definitely cut energy bills.
questions.explanation: That is the measured result described in the passage. Electricity savings and expansion are not established.

lessons.title: Listen: follow the signposts
lessons.description: Identify a presentation’s purpose, qualification, and recommendation.
lessons.listeningText: Today I will outline our four-day working week trial. At first, managers worried that customers would receive slower replies. In fact, average response times stayed the same, while staff reported less stress. That said, the trial involved only one department during a relatively quiet period. We should therefore avoid assuming that every team would obtain the same results. My recommendation is to run a second trial during the busy season before introducing a permanent change.

content.heading: Use signposts to follow structure
content.text: In presentations, phrases such as at first, in fact, that said, and therefore show how ideas relate. Note a few words under headings: concern, finding, limitation, and recommendation. You can often follow the argument even when an individual word is unfamiliar.
examples: At first introduces the original concern.
In fact introduces a finding that challenges it.
That said introduces a qualification.

content.heading: Hear the strength of a conclusion
content.text: A careful speaker distinguishes an observation from a general claim. In this account, one department’s results do not automatically apply to every team. Listen for caution words such as relatively and avoid assuming. The final recommendation may be further investigation rather than immediate action.
examples: Observation: average response times did not change.
Limitation: one department in a quiet period.
Recommendation: test the idea again during a busy season.

questions.prompt: What happened to average customer response times?
options: They were not observed at all.
questions.explanation: The speaker explicitly says average response times stayed the same.

questions.prompt: Why is the speaker cautious about the results?
options: The trial covered only one department in a quiet period.
questions.explanation: The limited setting makes generalization uncertain.

questions.prompt: What does the speaker recommend?
options: A second trial during the busy season
questions.explanation: The final sentence recommends another trial before a permanent change.

lessons.title: Make an essay easy to follow
lessons.description: Plan a position, develop paragraphs, and link ideas naturally.

content.heading: Answer the exact question
content.text: Before writing an opinion essay, identify the topic, the task, and any limits in the question. A question asking whether the benefits outweigh the drawbacks needs an overall judgement, not just two lists. Plan an introduction with your position, focused body paragraphs, and a conclusion that answers the question consistently.
examples: Question: Do the benefits of remote work outweigh the drawbacks?
Position: Overall, the flexibility is beneficial when teams maintain regular contact.
Body ideas: access and flexibility; communication problems and how to manage them.

content.heading: Develop instead of decorating
content.text: Explain how and why each point supports your position. Use a specific example and acknowledge a relevant limitation. Connect ideas by clear references and logical order; do not depend on a memorized connector at the start of every sentence. Write a short practice essay, then check whether each paragraph advances your answer.
examples: This flexibility can help parents arrange their working day.
However, new employees may need more direct support.
Regular mentoring sessions can reduce that difficulty.

questions.prompt: An “outweigh” question requires you to…
options: judge whether one side is more significant overall.
questions.explanation: Outweigh asks for a comparison and an overall judgement.

questions.prompt: Which paragraph plan provides development?
options: Four unrelated opinions → a long quotation
Point → explanation → specific example → link to the argument
questions.explanation: Explaining and illustrating a point shows how it supports the argument.

questions.prompt: What should the conclusion normally do?
options: Restate the overall answer supported by the essay.
questions.explanation: A conclusion draws together the position developed in the body.

lessons.title: Discuss both sides thoughtfully
lessons.description: Develop IELTS-style discussion answers with reasons and nuance.

content.heading: Move from personal to general
content.text: Discussion questions often ask about society rather than only your own life. State a general view, explain a cause or effect, and use a relevant example. Qualify broad statements with many, some, often, or in certain situations. This makes your answer more precise and gives you room to consider exceptions.
examples: Many people value flexible working because it reduces commuting.
For example, parents may find it easier to manage school pickups.
However, the benefits depend partly on the type of job.

content.heading: Acknowledge another perspective
content.text: You can recognize a reasonable opposing point without abandoning your position. Explain when that perspective applies, then state your own judgement. In an IELTS-style discussion, focus on relevant, developed answers and clear delivery. Memorized speeches can make it harder to respond to the actual question.
examples: I can see why some employers prefer office work.
That may be true for tasks requiring close collaboration.
On balance, I think a flexible approach works best.

questions.prompt: Which answer makes the most careful generalization?
options: Many commuters would welcome shorter journeys.
All jobs can be done online.
questions.explanation: Many makes a supported, limited generalization rather than an absolute claim.

questions.prompt: What does “I can see why some people disagree” do?
options: It proves your own opinion is wrong.
It changes the topic to eyesight.
questions.explanation: The phrase recognizes a contrasting view and can introduce a balanced discussion.

questions.prompt: What is the best preparation for an unfamiliar discussion question?
options: Practise giving a view, a reason, an example, and a qualification.
Recite a fixed speech regardless of the topic.
Use the longest words you know.
questions.explanation: A flexible answer structure helps you respond to the actual question.

lessons.title: Control emphasis & uncertainty
lessons.description: Use inversion, deduction, and cautious claims accurately.

content.heading: Emphasize with controlled inversion
content.text: After a negative or restrictive expression at the beginning of a clause, formal English often inverts the auxiliary and subject. If there is no auxiliary, use do, does, or did. Inversion adds emphasis; using it too often can sound unnatural. Keep the meaning clear before choosing a more complex structure.
examples: Rarely do we see such consistent results.
Not until Friday did the team reach an agreement.
Only after reviewing the data did she change her view.

content.heading: Calibrate a deduction
content.text: Must have plus a past participle expresses a strong deduction about the past; might have expresses a possibility; can’t have expresses a deduction that something was impossible. These describe your reasoning, not certainty based on direct observation. In academic work, may, appears to, and is likely to can help match a claim to its evidence.
examples: The lights were on; someone must have been inside.
The message might have gone to the wrong address.
The results appear to support the hypothesis.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct inversion.
options: Rarely we have seen such progress.
Rarely have seen we such progress.
Rarely have we seen such progress.
Rarely we seen have such progress.
questions.explanation: After initial rarely, put the auxiliary have before the subject we.

questions.prompt: Which sentence expresses a possible past explanation rather than a strong deduction?
options: I saw her miss the train.
She might have missed the train.
She must have missed the train.
questions.explanation: Might have expresses possibility; must have expresses a strong deduction.

questions.prompt: A small preliminary study suggests a benefit. Which claim is best calibrated?
options: There cannot be any other explanation.
The findings suggest a possible benefit that warrants further study.
The treatment always works for everyone.
The study proves that no further research is needed.
questions.explanation: A preliminary result supports a cautious claim rather than universal certainty.

lessons.title: Express nuance without vagueness
lessons.description: Use academic collocations, hedging, and precise word choice.

content.heading: Choose the exact relationship
content.text: Advanced vocabulary helps distinguish relationships. A correlation is an association between variables; it does not by itself establish causation. A feasible plan can be carried out in practice; an effective plan achieves its goal. Learn precise definitions alongside common combinations so your vocabulary strengthens the reasoning.
examples: a strong correlation between two measures
a feasible alternative to the current system
an effective intervention that reduced waiting times

content.heading: Hedge with a purpose
content.text: A hedge limits the strength or scope of a claim. Use tends to for a general pattern, to some extent for a partial truth, and arguably for a defensible interpretation. Avoid piling up hedges until your meaning disappears. Select the phrase that represents the actual uncertainty.
examples: The policy tends to benefit larger organizations.
This is arguably the most practical option.
The results are broadly consistent with earlier findings.

questions.prompt: A feasible proposal is one that…
questions.explanation: Feasible means possible and practical to implement.

questions.prompt: A correlation between exercise and wellbeing establishes…
options: an association, without proving causation by itself.
that exercise is the only cause of wellbeing.
questions.explanation: Correlation describes an association; causal claims need additional evidence.

questions.prompt: Which sentence states a cautious general pattern clearly?
options: The policy maybe could possibly perhaps do something.
The policy always benefits every company.
The policy tends to benefit larger companies.
questions.explanation: Tends to expresses a general pattern while allowing exceptions.

lessons.title: Read between the policy lines
lessons.description: Identify assumptions, qualifications, and the limits of a claim.

content.heading: Read a qualified recommendation
content.text: Read this analysis: “A subsidy for electric bicycles may reduce short car journeys, provided it reaches people who would otherwise drive. Purchases by existing cyclists could increase sales without reducing traffic. The programme should therefore be evaluated against changes in travel behaviour rather than sales alone. A rise in sales would be encouraging, but insufficient evidence of environmental benefit.” Notice the condition attached to the potential benefit.
examples: Desired outcome: fewer short car journeys.
Necessary condition in the argument: some purchasers would otherwise drive.
Sales are an intermediate measure, not the final outcome.

content.heading: Test the link in the reasoning
content.text: A writer may distinguish an indicator from the goal it is supposed to represent. Ask what would need to be true for the evidence to support the conclusion. Read conditional language carefully: may and provided do not promise an outcome. Summarize both the proposal and the limit in one sentence.
examples: More bicycle sales do not automatically mean fewer car trips.
Travel behaviour is the recommended evaluation measure.
The writer supports evaluation rather than claiming certain success.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, why are sales alone an insufficient measure?
options: No one wants an electric bicycle.
Buyers may already cycle instead of drive.
questions.explanation: Purchases by existing cyclists could increase sales without replacing car trips.

questions.prompt: What does “provided it reaches…” introduce?
options: An established result of the programme
A guarantee that all drivers will change
A condition on the potential benefit
questions.explanation: Provided means on the condition that; the benefit depends on reaching the relevant users.

questions.prompt: Which summary best represents the writer’s stance?
options: The subsidy should be judged only by sales.
Electric bicycles cannot ever benefit a city.
The subsidy may help, but evaluation must establish whether travel behaviour changes.
The subsidy will certainly eliminate traffic.
questions.explanation: This preserves both the possible benefit and the requirement for outcome-based evaluation.

lessons.title: Listen: a lecture with a qualification
lessons.description: Take efficient notes and distinguish findings from interpretation.
lessons.listeningText: A common assumption is that taking more notes always leads to better learning. Yet the amount written may be less important than the processing involved. In our classroom study, students who summarized ideas in their own words performed better on conceptual questions than students who copied sentences. I should stress, however, that the groups did not differ on simple factual recall. Moreover, the study took place in a single introductory course. The findings are therefore promising, but we should be cautious about extending them to all subjects or age groups.

content.heading: Build notes around relationships
content.text: For academic listening, record the main claim, evidence, qualification, and implication. Use abbreviations or arrows rather than trying to transcribe the lecture. In this extract, the speaker contrasts the quantity of notes with the depth of processing. Pay attention when the speaker says yet or however.
examples: Assumption: more notes → better learning.
Finding: own-word summaries → stronger conceptual answers.
No difference: simple factual recall.

content.heading: Keep the boundary of the finding
content.text: An observed difference on one kind of test is not a difference on every kind of test. A study in one course may not generalize to all learners. In IELTS-style listening practice, identify exactly what the speaker claims, not what you expect the lecture to say. Use the transcript only after a first independent listen.
examples: Conceptual understanding and factual recall are different outcomes.
Single course = a limit on generalization.
Promising does not mean conclusive.

questions.prompt: What did own-word summaries improve in the study?
questions.explanation: The reported advantage was on conceptual questions.

questions.prompt: What did the speaker say about simple factual recall?
questions.explanation: The qualification explicitly says there was no difference on factual recall.

questions.prompt: Why should the findings be generalized cautiously?
options: The study was conducted in a single introductory course.
Students were not allowed to take notes.
questions.explanation: A study in one course does not establish the same effect across all subjects and age groups.

lessons.title: IELTS Writing Task 2: a clear position
lessons.description: Respond fully, sustain an argument, and revise for clarity.

content.heading: Analyze and plan before you draft
content.text: In IELTS Academic Writing Task 2, write at least 250 words and allow about 40 of the writing test’s 60 minutes. Read every part of the prompt. For “Discuss both views and give your opinion,” explain both positions and make your own judgement clear. A fixed paragraph count is less important than a complete, logically developed answer.
examples: Prompt: Some favour university funding; others prefer vocational training. Discuss both views and give your opinion.
Plan both views before deciding how to organize them.
Position: Public funding should support both routes according to local needs.

content.heading: Develop and qualify your reasoning
content.text: Support each main idea with an explanation and a relevant example, then relate it to the question. Consider a limitation when it improves the argument. Avoid unsupported sweeping claims and memorized introductions that could fit any topic. Review your response for task coverage, paragraph progression, precise vocabulary, grammar, and punctuation.
examples: University research can benefit industries beyond the campus.
Vocational programmes can address immediate shortages in skilled trades.
The appropriate balance may vary with regional employment needs.

questions.prompt: What does “Discuss both views and give your opinion” require?
options: Explain only the view you agree with.
Explain both views and give your own clear judgement.
questions.explanation: All three elements are part of the task: both views and your opinion.

questions.prompt: What is the minimum word requirement for IELTS Academic Writing Task 2?
questions.explanation: Task 2 requires at least 250 words; about 40 minutes is the recommended allocation.

questions.prompt: Which claim is best suited to a careful academic argument?
options: All countries need precisely the same funding policy.
The balance of funding should reflect educational goals and local employment needs.
University is useless for every student.
questions.explanation: The final claim is specific, qualified, and open to reasoned support.

lessons.title: Speak with range & control
lessons.description: Develop a long turn and handle abstract follow-up questions.

content.heading: Prepare a flexible long turn
content.text: For an IELTS-style long turn, make brief notes that help you cover the topic: context, key details, significance, and reflection. Speak from the notes instead of writing a script. A small specific event is often easier to develop than a grand but vague story. Use time references and linking phrases to guide the listener.
examples: Topic: a person who taught you something useful.
Context: my first week at a new job.
Reflection: I learned that asking questions can prevent mistakes.

content.heading: Think aloud with a clear direction
content.text: Abstract follow-up questions may ask about causes, social effects, or future change. Give a provisional view, develop it, and qualify it when needed. It is acceptable to take a brief thinking pause. Use complex language where it helps, while preserving clear rhythm, intelligible pronunciation, and a direct answer.
examples: My initial view is that practical experience is essential.
That said, some skills need a strong theoretical foundation.
The balance probably depends on the profession.

questions.prompt: Which set of notes best supports a flexible long turn?
options: A full essay to read word for word
Context, key event, useful details, personal reflection
questions.explanation: Brief content notes support organization while allowing natural speech.

questions.prompt: How can you respond to an abstract follow-up question?
options: Say a memorized introduction for every topic.
Give a view, develop its reasoning, and acknowledge a relevant limit.
Repeat your previous story regardless of the question.
questions.explanation: This structure develops an answer while maintaining relevance and nuance.

questions.prompt: Which use of sophisticated language is most effective?
options: Choosing precise expressions and structures that make your ideas easier to follow
Using every complex structure in every sentence
Using unfamiliar idioms even when the meaning is uncertain
Speaking so quickly that details are unclear
questions.explanation: Range is useful when it supports accurate and intelligible communication.

lessons.title: Fine-tune time, stance & implication
lessons.description: Use mixed conditionals and aspect to express exact meanings.

content.heading: Connect an unreal past to the present
content.text: A mixed conditional can link a counterfactual past situation to a present consequence. Use if plus past perfect for the unreal past condition, and would plus base verb for a present result. The time relationship determines the structure; do not force every conditional into a single memorized pattern.
examples: If I had accepted that job, I would live abroad now.
If we had invested in training, the team would be more confident today.
Had I known about the delay, I would not be waiting here now.

content.heading: Let aspect express your focus
content.text: Compare a completed result with an activity continuing up to a reference point. The present perfect simple can foreground an achieved amount; the continuous often foregrounds duration or ongoing effort. Context, the verb’s meaning, and the intended focus all matter. Some verbs describing states do not normally use the continuous.
examples: I have written three reports. → completed amount
I have been writing reports all morning. → activity and duration
I have known her for years. → state, normally not continuous

questions.prompt: Which sentence links an unreal past choice to a present situation?
options: If I had taken the job, I would live in London now.
If I had taken the job, I would have moved then.
If I study tomorrow, I will pass.
If I were free now, I would help.
questions.explanation: Had taken describes the unreal past; would live now describes its imagined present result.

questions.prompt: Which sentence foregrounds a completed quantity?
options: I have been writing reports all morning.
I was writing when you called.
questions.explanation: The present perfect simple with three reports emphasizes the achieved amount.

questions.prompt: Which is the most natural neutral statement about a continuing state?
options: I have known her for years.
I have been knowing her for years.
questions.explanation: Know is normally a state verb, so the present perfect simple is natural here.

lessons.title: Connotation, register & exact intent
lessons.description: Choose language for its implications as well as its definition.

content.heading: Hear the judgement inside the word
content.text: Words can share a basic meaning while expressing a different attitude. Economical suggests sensible use of money; stingy criticizes an unwillingness to spend. Assertive can be positive; aggressive often suggests excessive force. Before choosing a synonym, consider what judgement it implies about the person or action.
examples: She is economical with resources. → approving efficiency
He is stingy with his time. → criticism
The proposal is ambitious. → potentially admiring, depending on context

content.heading: Use plain precision when it serves best
content.text: Mastery includes knowing when a simple expression is the most exact one. Avoid idioms that create ambiguity in international or technical communication. In sensitive feedback, describe observable behaviour and its effect instead of assigning a hostile label. Match the strength of your word to the strength of the evidence.
examples: Instead of “You are careless”: “The report omitted two required figures.”
Instead of “Get the ball rolling”: “Start the review on Monday.”
“Inconsistent” is more precise than “terrible” when results vary.

questions.prompt: Which word usually expresses a negative judgement about unwillingness to spend?
questions.explanation: Stingy is generally disapproving, while economical often praises sensible use of resources.

questions.prompt: Which feedback is the most specific and actionable?
options: The report omits the two figures requested in the brief.
questions.explanation: It identifies an observable issue that the writer can correct.

questions.prompt: Why might “Start the review on Monday” be preferable to “Get the ball rolling”?
options: It states the action and timing clearly for an international audience.
Plain language is always less advanced.
questions.explanation: The direct wording reduces ambiguity while preserving the intended meaning.

lessons.title: Read a sophisticated argument critically
lessons.description: Analyze framing, counterarguments, and conclusions across a text.

content.heading: Track what the writer accepts and rejects
content.text: Read this commentary: “It would be convenient to treat every increase in productivity as a rise in wellbeing. Yet a measure of output says little about how gains are distributed or whether workers have more control over their time. This is not an argument against productivity growth; it is a warning against treating one indicator as a complete account of social progress. The question is how growth translates into better lives, and for whom.” Identify the distinction that drives the argument.
examples: Accepted: productivity growth may be valuable.
Rejected: productivity alone fully measures social progress.
Central questions: distribution, control, and lived outcomes.

content.heading: Preserve the scope when summarizing
content.text: A strong summary captures the writer’s position without converting a qualification into a rejection. Pay attention to not every, little, alone, and complete: these words control the scope of a claim. Ask which conclusion follows from the text and which would require additional evidence.
examples: “Output says little about distribution” does not mean output has no value.
The writer questions the adequacy of a measure.
The passage does not establish that productivity growth always harms workers.

questions.prompt: What is the writer primarily challenging?
options: The use of productivity as a complete measure of social progress
questions.explanation: The target is treating one indicator as a complete account, not productivity growth itself.

questions.prompt: Which claim would misrepresent the passage?
options: Control over time is relevant to workers’ lives.
The writer believes productivity growth should always be opposed.
Distribution affects how growth benefits people.
Output alone may not describe wellbeing adequately.
questions.explanation: The writer explicitly says this is not an argument against productivity growth.

questions.prompt: Which question best extends the writer’s reasoning?
options: Why should workers have no leisure?
Who receives the gains from increased output, and how do their lives change?
How can output figures be printed in a larger font?
Can every other measure be removed?
questions.explanation: This follows the passage’s focus on distribution and the translation of growth into wellbeing.

lessons.title: Listen: the meaning beyond the words
lessons.description: Interpret diplomatic disagreement and distinguish inference from fact.
lessons.listeningText: The proposed launch date is certainly ambitious. I appreciate why the sales team would like to announce the product before the conference. My concern is that the accessibility review has not yet been completed, and rushing it could leave us fixing avoidable problems after release. If the review comes back clear next week, the timetable may still be achievable. Until then, I would be reluctant to promise that date publicly. Perhaps we could prepare the announcement now while keeping the release date provisional.

content.heading: Recognize a diplomatic objection
content.text: In professional discussion, a speaker may acknowledge another team’s goal before raising a concern. Listen to the whole turn rather than interpreting a positive opening as agreement. Here, certainly ambitious is followed by a concrete risk and a condition. The speaker proposes a way forward without making an unconditional commitment.
examples: Acknowledgement: the sales team has a reason for the timing.
Concern: the accessibility review is incomplete.
Stance: avoid a public promise until the risk is clearer.

content.heading: Separate intended meaning from invented detail
content.text: A reasonable inference is supported by the speaker’s words and context. It is not permission to invent motives or facts. The speaker is cautious about the date, but does not say the product has already failed a review. Track what is conditional, what is established, and what remains unknown.
examples: Established: the review has not finished.
Conditional: the timetable may work if the review is clear.
Proposed compromise: prepare the announcement with a provisional date.

questions.prompt: What is the speaker’s overall stance toward the launch date?
options: Cautious acceptance only if the unresolved review permits it
A demand to cancel the product permanently
questions.explanation: The speaker allows that the date may be achievable but does not want to promise it before the review.

questions.prompt: Which statement is established by the recording?
options: The product has failed the accessibility review.
The accessibility review is not yet complete.
The sales team refuses any compromise.
questions.explanation: The speaker explicitly says the review has not yet been completed.

questions.prompt: What compromise does the speaker propose?
options: Prepare the announcement while keeping the release date provisional.
questions.explanation: This preserves useful preparation without making an unsupported public commitment.

lessons.title: IELTS Task 1: make the overview count
lessons.description: Select key features, compare data accurately, and edit with purpose.

content.heading: Summarize rather than list
content.text: IELTS Academic Writing Task 1 asks for at least 150 words, with about 20 minutes recommended. For a chart, identify the main trends, largest differences, and meaningful exceptions. Include an overview and select figures that support it. Describe what the information shows; avoid inventing reasons that the chart does not establish.
examples: Practice data: cycling to work, 2010 → 2020: Town A 10% → 25%; Town B 20% → 22%; Town C 30% → 28%.
Overview: A rose sharply, B changed little, and C declined slightly.
Town C remained the highest of the three in 2020.

content.heading: Compare accurately and revise ruthlessly
content.text: Distinguish a percentage-point change from a relative percentage change. Moving from 10% to 25% is a rise of 15 percentage points, not 15 percent. Group related figures instead of writing a separate isolated sentence for every value. During revision, remove repetition, verify comparisons, and make each reference unambiguous.
examples: Town A increased by 15 percentage points.
By contrast, Town C fell from 30% to 28%.
Town B rose only slightly, from 20% to 22%.

questions.prompt: Which overview accurately describes the practice data?
options: Town A remained the lowest in 2020.
Town A rose substantially, B rose slightly, and C fell slightly.
Town B overtook every other town.
questions.explanation: The overview correctly captures the direction and relative scale of each change.

questions.prompt: How much did Town A’s cycling share rise, from 10% to 25%?
questions.explanation: 25 minus 10 is 15 percentage points. The relative increase is 150%, a different calculation.

questions.prompt: Which sentence should be excluded unless further evidence is supplied?
options: Town A’s increase was caused by a new cycle lane.
Town C had the highest share in 2020.
Town A recorded the largest increase.
questions.explanation: The figures establish a change, but provide no evidence about its cause.

lessons.title: Respond with precision & flexibility
lessons.description: Handle challenging questions and adapt your message to the listener.

content.heading: Define the issue before judging it
content.text: A broad question may contain an unclear term or a false choice. Briefly explain how you understand the issue, then answer directly. Distinguish contexts instead of forcing a simple yes or no. This is especially useful in advanced discussion and IELTS-style follow-up questions, where the quality of your reasoning supports a developed answer.
examples: If by success we mean long-term wellbeing, income is only one factor.
For routine tasks, automation can help; in sensitive decisions, human oversight remains important.
I would distinguish access to information from the ability to evaluate it.

content.heading: Adapt without losing precision
content.text: Explain the same idea to a friend, a colleague, and a non-specialist. Change the terminology and detail while preserving the meaning. Use stress and pauses to highlight the contrast that matters. End with a clear judgement when the question asks for one, rather than continuing until the main point disappears.
examples: Technical: The sample may not be representative.
Plain: The people surveyed may not reflect the wider population.
Judgement: I support the proposal, provided the evaluation includes those most affected.

questions.prompt: Which response handles a broad question about success most thoughtfully?
options: If success means long-term wellbeing, income matters but is not the only factor.
Success is success because it is successful.
There is no way to discuss the topic.
Success has exactly the same meaning for everyone.
questions.explanation: It defines the key term and gives a qualified, relevant position.

questions.prompt: What does adapting an explanation to a non-specialist involve?
options: Changing the facts to make them entertaining
Using accessible wording while preserving the precise meaning
questions.explanation: Adaptation changes presentation, not the underlying accuracy.

questions.prompt: Which ending gives a clear but qualified judgement?
options: I have no conclusion after all.
Overall, I support the proposal if the evaluation includes those most affected.
There are words and more words.
questions.explanation: The ending states a position and the condition attached to it.

lessons.title: Professional Correspondence
lessons.description: Master the tone and structure of formal business emails.

content.heading: Formal vs Informal Tone
content.text: In business, the tone depends on your relationship with the reader. Use "Dear [Name]" for formal first contacts and "Hi [Name]" for established colleagues. Avoid contractions like "don’t" or "can’t" in high-level formal reports, but use them in internal team emails to sound natural.
examples: Formal: I would appreciate it if you could respond.
Informal: Let me know what you think.
Semi-formal: Could you please check the file?

content.heading: The Structure of a Request
content.text: A professional request follows a clear path: Greeting → Context → The Request → Call to Action → Closing. Be direct but polite. Use modal verbs like "could" and "would" to soften requests so they do not sound like orders.
examples: I am writing to follow up on...
Would it be possible to reschedule?
I look forward to hearing from you.

questions.prompt: Which greeting is most appropriate for a first-time formal email to a CEO?
options: To whom it may concern (without a name)
questions.explanation: Dear [Title] [Surname] is the standard for formal first contacts.

questions.prompt: Change this to be more professional: “Send me the report now.”
options: Could you please send me the report at your earliest convenience?
questions.explanation: Using “Could you please” and “at your earliest convenience” creates a polite, professional request.

questions.prompt: Which closing is best for a formal business letter?
questions.explanation: Sincerely or Yours faithfully are the standard formal closings.

lessons.title: Effective Meeting Leadership
lessons.description: Manage discussions, interrupt politely, and summarize agreements.

content.heading: Opening and Setting the Agenda
content.text: A good meeting starts with a clear purpose. Use "signposting" phrases to tell listeners where the conversation is going. Instead of just starting, say "The goal of today’s meeting is to..." or "First, we will look at...". This keeps the team focused and professional.
examples: Our main objective today is...
I’ve divided the agenda into three parts.
Let’s start by reviewing the previous minutes.

content.heading: Polite Interruption and Steering
content.text: In a meeting, you may need to stop someone or move the topic. Use "softeners" to avoid sounding rude. Phrases like "If I could just jump in here" or "That’s a great point, but moving back to the main topic..." allow you to maintain control while respecting others.
examples: Sorry to interrupt, but...
Could we just clarify one point before moving on?
I think we’ve covered this; let’s move to the next item.

questions.prompt: What is the best way to start a meeting professionally?
options: The goal of today’s meeting is to decide on the budget.
Stop talking and listen to me.
