questions.explanation: Clearly stating the objective (goal) sets a professional tone.

questions.prompt: How do you politely interrupt a colleague who is talking too long?
options: Sorry to interrupt, but could we just clarify this point?
questions.explanation: Apologizing first and asking to clarify is a professional way to steer the conversation.

questions.prompt: Which phrase is used for “signposting” the agenda?
options: First, we will review the results, then we will discuss the plan.
questions.explanation: Signposting tells the listener the sequence of events (First... then...).

lessons.title: Writing a Project Proposal
lessons.description: Structure a persuasive business case with a clear ROI.

content.heading: The Executive Summary
content.text: The most important part of a proposal is the summary. Busy managers often read only this section. It must contain the Problem, the Solution, and the Result (ROI - Return on Investment). Keep it to one page and use bullet points for key benefits to make it scannable.
examples: Problem: Current shipping costs are too high.
Solution: Switch to a regional logistics partner.
Result: Estimated 15% reduction in monthly costs.

content.heading: Justifying the Cost
content.text: Do not just ask for money; explain why it is an investment. Use data-driven language. Instead of "It will be better," use "It will increase efficiency by 20%." Contrast the cost of the solution with the cost of doing nothing (the cost of inaction).
examples: Investment: £5,000 for new software.
Gain: 10 hours of saved labor per week.
Risk of inaction: Continued data errors and lost revenue.

questions.prompt: What is the primary purpose of an Executive Summary?
options: To list every single detail of the project.
To provide a high-level overview of the problem, solution, and result.
To explain the history of the company.
questions.explanation: The summary is for busy decision-makers to see the core value quickly.

questions.prompt: Which statement is more persuasive in a proposal?
options: This software is really good and we like it.
This software will reduce manual entry errors by 30%.
We think the software might help us.
The software is very expensive but nice.
questions.explanation: Data-driven claims (30% reduction) are more persuasive than subjective opinions.

questions.prompt: What does “ROI” stand for in a business context?
questions.explanation: Return on Investment measures the gain or loss generated on an investment relative to the amount of money invested.

placementQuestions.explanation: Use I am to describe yourself.

placementQuestions.prompt: There are three ___ on the table.
placementQuestions.explanation: After three, use the plural books.
The present simple takes s with she: walks.
Last Sunday is a finished past time, so use visited.

options: This bag is lighter than mine.
This bag is lighter as mine.
This bag is more light than mine.
placementQuestions.explanation: Use lighter than to compare the weight of two bags.

placementQuestions.prompt: I ___ here since 2020, and I still live here.
placementQuestions.explanation: The present perfect with since connects a starting point in the past to now.

placementQuestions.prompt: If I finish my work early tomorrow, I ___ you.
placementQuestions.explanation: For a real future possibility, use if plus present simple and will plus base verb.

placementQuestions.prompt: The report ___ by two experts before it was published.
placementQuestions.explanation: Had been reviewed is the past perfect passive: the review preceded publication.

placementQuestions.prompt: A study finds an association between two variables. What can it establish by itself?
options: The variables are related in the observed data.
The relationship applies to every person.
placementQuestions.explanation: An association alone does not establish causation or universal applicability.

options: Only then she understood the problem.
Only then understood she the problem.
Only then did she understand the problem.
Only then did she understood the problem.
placementQuestions.explanation: Initial only then triggers auxiliary-subject inversion; after did, use understand.

placementQuestions.prompt: Which sentence links an unreal past event with a present consequence?
options: If she calls tomorrow, I will answer.
If she had called, I would have answered then.
If she had accepted the post, she would be living abroad now.
placementQuestions.explanation: The past perfect condition combines with a present imagined result: would be living now.

placementQuestions.prompt: An author says, “These findings are promising, though the sample is narrow.” Which paraphrase preserves the stance?
options: The author rejects the findings entirely.
The sample makes any observation impossible.
The results are encouraging, but their wider applicability remains uncertain.
The findings prove the theory for everyone.
placementQuestions.explanation: The author expresses cautious optimism while limiting generalization.

words.meaning: A greeting used when you meet someone or begin a conversation.
words.example: Hello, my name is Maya.

words.meaning: A person who studies at a school, college, or in another learning setting.
words.example: I am an English student.

words.meaning: Someone you know well and like spending time with.
words.example: My friend and I read together.

words.meaning: On most occasions; as a normal habit.
words.example: I usually study after breakfast.

words.meaning: The area around your home or a particular part of a town.
words.example: There is a library in my neighbourhood.

words.meaning: To take and use something with permission, intending to return it.
words.example: May I borrow your pen for a minute?

words.meaning: An arrangement to keep a seat, room, or table for someone.
words.example: I have a reservation for two nights.

words.meaning: Happening or arriving later than planned.
words.example: Our train is delayed by twenty minutes.

words.meaning: Physically relaxed or free from discomfort.
words.example: This chair is more comfortable than that one.

words.meaning: The latest time or date by which something must be completed.
words.example: We need to meet the deadline on Friday.

words.meaning: Information or observations that support a belief or conclusion.
words.example: Look for evidence before accepting the claim.

words.meaning: A duty to deal with something or be accountable for it.
words.example: She took responsibility for organizing the event.

words.meaning: Important or large enough to deserve attention in a particular context.
words.example: The new timetable made a significant difference to commuters.

words.meaning: A detail that limits or modifies a claim; also a credential showing training.
words.example: The speaker added a qualification: the trial involved only one team.

words.meaning: Temporary or arranged for now, and subject to later confirmation.
words.example: The release date is provisional until the review is complete.

words.meaning: Possible and practical to carry out.
words.example: We need a feasible plan that fits our budget.

words.meaning: An association between variables, which alone does not prove a causal relationship.
words.example: The study found a correlation between the two measures.

words.meaning: To support a statement with evidence or facts.
words.example: The report needs data to substantiate its main claim.

words.meaning: A small but meaningful difference in meaning, feeling, or expression.
words.example: Her explanation captured the nuance of the disagreement.

words.meaning: An additional feeling or judgement suggested by a word beyond its basic definition.
words.example: Stingy has a more negative connotation than economical.

words.meaning: Describing an imagined situation that differs from what actually happened.
words.example: The counterfactual question considers what would have happened without the policy.

words.meaning: Open to more than one interpretation, or not clearly supporting one conclusion.
words.example: The evidence was equivocal, so the team avoided a firm conclusion.

words.meaning: Showing careful judgement in noticing differences and evaluating quality.
words.example: A discerning reader checks the strength of the supporting evidence.

words.meaning: Expressed clearly in few words, without unnecessary detail.
words.example: She gave a succinct summary of a complex argument.
